topStories.headline: Polk Street's Fall Food Wave Is Mostly Still Coming — One Counter Is Open, Four Are Not
topStories.dek: As of early October, five food and drink projects have been announced along the Russian Hill and Polk Gulch stretch of Polk Street, but only one has opened its doors.
topStories.body:
As of the first week of October 2026, five food and drink projects have been announced along the Russian Hill and Polk Gulch stretch of Polk Street, according to food writer Jeff Marples. One is open; the other four are at different stages of permitted, delayed, or slated — and the lineup skews heavily toward breakfast and lunch.

The one spot already serving customers is Handroll Hawker, which opened September 29 at 2360 Polk St. at the corner of Union. The counter-service restaurant, described by the SF Standard as San Francisco's first Australian-style handroll spot, serves palm-size, cylindrical sushi rolls meant to be eaten on the move, taken out, or finished at one of a handful of tables. The menu spans salmon and avocado, tempura shrimp, and spicy tuna.

Also in the pipeline is Bageletto, the Mission bagel shop that plans to open a sit-down café at 2193 Polk St. — the former Peet's between Broadway and Vallejo — with fresh bagels delivered twice daily from its 14th Street kitchen in small batches. Co-founder Kiki Theodorides told the SF Standard the team was targeting a 60-to-90-day window from spring, which puts the opening well into fall; no firm date has been published.

Marples notes that looking at what each project plans to serve tells its own story: the bakery, the bagel shop, the coffee counter, and the hand-roll spot are all built for the hours before dinner. The picture that emerges is a Polk corridor splitting in two this fall — daytime action on the street level, evenings on the hill.

topStories.headline: A Humphrey Bogart Filming Location in Russian Hill Could Gain Eight New Apartments
topStories.dek: City planners have published a pre-application proposal to add three stories of housing above the garage of the historic Tamalpais Apartments at 1201 Greenwich Street.
topStories.body:
Plans surfaced this week for a potential residential expansion at 1201 Greenwich Street in Russian Hill — the Tamalpais Apartments, an 11-story tower with a film noir pedigree that predates this proposal by decades. San Francisco YIMBY first reported the filing on October 10; Hoodline followed the same day.

The proposal, drafted by San Francisco-based Syncopated Architecture, calls for a three-story vertical addition above the existing garage section of the building. The plans would add eight apartments across 13,140 square feet — five three-bedroom units and three four-bedroom units — while reducing parking capacity by just one space, from 26 to 25. The new housing is designed to wrap around the historic 1923 structure without altering it.

The Tamalpais Apartments has a cinematic history that long predates the proposal. Its fire escape and entrance appeared in pivotal scenes of the 1947 Bogart thriller Dark Passage and the 1952 Joan Crawford film Sudden Fear, according to Hoodline. The tower was designed by architect Conrad A. Meussdorffer, who operated his own studio from 1897 through 1939.

The plans were published by the city's planning department ahead of a project review meeting — a step that precedes any formal application. The future development could invoke the city's Housing Choice Program. No estimated cost or construction timeline has been established.

topStories.headline: Chinatown's Him Mark Lai Library Prepares to Close for a 30-Month, $47.8 Million Renovation
topStories.dek: Construction on the 1921 Carnegie branch is expected to begin this fall, with services relocating two blocks away to 950 Grant Avenue for the duration of the rebuild.
topStories.body:
The Chinatown/Him Mark Lai Branch Library at 1135 Powell Street is preparing to close its doors for a major renovation this fall, with construction expected to run approximately 30 months, according to the San Francisco Public Library and SF Public Works. The project carries a budget of $47.8 million.

The Public Works Commission approved the construction contract at its July 23 hearing, with the contractor selected through a competitive bidding process. During construction, library services will relocate to a temporary branch on the ground floor of a commercial building two blocks away, at 950 Grant Avenue.

The scope of the renovation is extensive. Plans call for restoring the grand reading room to its original architectural character — reversing changes made during a 1995 seismic retrofit that diminished the landmarked space — as well as adding a new community room that can seat up to 100 people, a dedicated teen area, a larger children's room, a public roof terrace, a gallery celebrating Chinese and Asian American history, and a new elevator. The renovated building will be required to achieve USGBC LEED Gold certification.

The library project is the third leg of a $150 million construction push reshaping central Chinatown, alongside the $73 million Portsmouth Square renovation — which broke ground in June and closed the park for an estimated two years — and a 30-month upgrade of the Chinatown Public Health Center, which sits atop the Broadway Tunnel. Merchants near Portsmouth Square have already reported significant disruption, including lost parking and reduced foot traffic, since that project began.

moreNews.headline: FITNESS SF to Open 42,000-Square-Foot Polk Gulch Gym on November 1
moreNews.body: FITNESS SF will open its newest location at 1600 Jackson Street in Polk Gulch on November 1, 2026, according to the company's website. The gym spans approximately 42,000 square feet and will offer group fitness classes, personal training, red light therapy, a traditional dry sauna, EGYM equipment, and free parking. Founding memberships are currently available at pre-sale pricing. The location is billed as serving the Polk Street corridor, including residents of Russian Hill and Nob Hill who previously lacked a neighborhood gym.

moreNews.headline: Broadway Tunnel Running at Half Capacity Through October 2027
moreNews.body: Drivers should continue to expect delays in the Broadway Tunnel through at least October 2027, according to a July 20 press release from SF Public Works. A partial closure — one lane available in each direction — began August 17, 2026, as part of seismic retrofitting and other upgrades at the Chinatown Public Health Center, which sits directly above the tunnel. The closure is one of three overlapping Chinatown construction projects that together carry a total cost of approximately $150 million. Motorists are encouraged to check SFMTA.com/ChinatownParking for alternate parking and transit information.
